To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) multivariate pattern analyses of MEG data can reveal the spatio-temporal neural dynamics underlying cognitive processes, and that (2) the results are largely comparable to those from EEG, but also reveal partly unique aspects of neural processing, which (3) have a distinct spatial distribution and (4) emerge earlier in time for multivariate MEG than for multivariate EEG.

multivariate pattern analyses of MEG/EEC data can reveal the spatio-temporal neural dynamics underlying cognition and that MEG and EEC offer complementary views on the neural processes underlying cognitive function.

multivariate pattern analysis of concurrent MEG and EEG recordings yields convergent and complementary results, and that the unique aspects of the two signals are associated with different neural generators in the visual system.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the neural dynamics that underlie cognition.
understanding how the brain represents information.
the representational dynamics in the human visual brain.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the MEG data is better for the early stages of processing and the EEG data is better for later stages of processing.
MEG and MEG data can be used to study the same neural processes and that the results of multivariant pattern classification analyses of MEG data are comparable to those from EEG data.
MEG and fMRI are complementary methods that can be used for the study of the neural correlates of visual perception and that the two methods can be used to complement and cross-validate each other.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
MEG and EEC have largely equivalent results, but also partly unique components.
MEG and EEC are both capable of capturing the spatio-temporal patterns of neural activation, but MEG has an advantage of capturing the earlier and lower-level aspects.
MEG and EEC have largely equivalent results, and that MEG has unique results that are complementary to EEG.
The main takeaway from our work is that
multivariate pattern analyses of MEG data yield largely similar results as EEG, and that the two modalities offer complimentary insights into the spatio-temporal organization of neural processing.
MEG and EEC data yield largely equivalent results in multivariate pattern analysis, and that the unique components of the two modalities can be localized to distinct cortical regions.
MEG and MEG offer largely equivalent information about neural representations.
